findings.where: Screens 1, 3 and 7 (One diode, Four diodes, The probe), opening state
findings.what: All three open with the cursor at 0°, a zero crossing, so the load reads "no current", the graph is empty, the live line says "no current flows" and the film of these screens shows nothing moving; open them at about 90° (270° for the probe) with the path bold and the dots flowing, or run a short sweep in, so the first picture is alive.

findings.where: Every SHOW screen, words plus the live line under the picture
findings.what: Screens 9 and 11 carry 87 and 89 words above the picture plus a 33-word live line and the 13-word graph note below it, about 133 words, and screens 1, 3, 5 and 7 reach 96 to 107 words before the note, so cut the live line on SHOW screens to one short sentence (drop its "Over the whole cycle..." tail, which repeats the legend) and trim screens 9 and 11.

The question asks about 440 V but the bench opens labelled "400 V 3-phase" with 400 V waves, so the only number in the picture contradicts the question; open it on 440 V and let the Check sweep in the 594 V average.
[^1] sits twice on paraphrased claims, including the bold closing summary, rather than on a rule or value he would look up; take it off the summary sentence.

findings.where: Screen 11 (Where 1.35 comes from) and the explain
findings.what: The lesson never says that this 1.35 is the one behind the "400 × 1.35 = 540 V" DC bus he was given with motor drives, so add one sentence such as "That is the 540 V bus inside a 400 V drive, and now you can see where it comes from."

"The area under that cosine slice is the peak × 2 sin 30°" skips the step from the integral, so add "The area under a cosine is a sine, so from −30° to +30° it is sin 30° − sin(−30°) = 1 times the peak."

The six pale line-to-line waves are unlabelled and the line voltages are not drawn, so "the highest line" in the words and the live line cannot be seen on the graph; label the top under the cursor with its pair (for example "L3 − L2") to tie it to the bold diodes.

findings.where: Screens 1, 5 and 7, end of the sweep and the still
findings.what: The sweeps and stills end at 360°, another zero crossing, so the finished bridge picture says "no current" and the live line opens "The supply is passing through zero"; end the still at 359° or keep the last path drawn.

findings.where: Screen 2 (The average at the end), question
findings.what: The premise, that the average reads 207 V at 180°, is only in the graph's small legend, so put "At 180° the average reads 207 V." in the question so it stands alone in the read-through.

findings.where: Screen 6 (What the diodes take), question and bench
findings.what: "How much voltage do its diodes take?" can be read per diode, which makes "About 0.7 V" defensible, and the bench shows a 230 V bridge for a 12 V charger; ask "How much lower is the output than with perfect diodes?" and balance the right answer, which is the longest.
The right answer is the only option with numbers and by far the longest, so it can be picked by its look; give the wrong options a comparable form.
"D3 and D4 conduct. They join D1 straight across the supply." credits both, but only D3 does it, by tying D1's top end to wire B, and saying so points him at the cause on the drawing.
The words lean on "the positive rail" and "the negative rail", but the drawing does not label them; mark the top and bottom wires "+ rail" and "− rail".

findings.where: Graph at 0°, screen 1 opening (360 px light)
findings.what: The cursor's dot sits on the end of the "0 V" axis label, so the label reads "0 V●"; nudge the label left or drop it while the cursor is at 0°.

findings.where: Note under the graph, all 13 screens
findings.what: "One supply cycle, 0° to 360°. The numbers are worked out, not measured." repeats 13 words after the diagram on every screen, so show it on screen 1 only.

findings.where: Screen 5 and the practice worked example, ripple
findings.what: Ripple is given only for 50 Hz, including a 440 V, 50 Hz example, though the same rule gives 120 Hz and 360 Hz on a 60 Hz supply, which is common at sea; add the 60 Hz figure in one clause.
